1a.fix: Slide 34 lists the condensed phases at 1000 K as Ni, NiO, \mathrm{Ni_3S_2} and \mathrm{NiSO_4}, but its own diagram has a fifth field, NiS, the largest sulphide field at high p_{\mathrm{SO_2}}. The condensed phases are Ni, \mathrm{Ni_3S_2}, NiS, NiO and \mathrm{NiSO_4}.
1a.html:
Definition. A predominance area diagram (Kellogg diagram) is an isothermal plot, drawn from thermodynamic data, of \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} for a metal-sulphur-oxygen system. It divides the plane into areas in which one condensed phase (metal, sulphide, oxide or sulphate) is stable in equilibrium with the gas. Lines are two-phase equilibria and the points where three lines meet are three-phase equilibria.

Construction (Ni-S-O at 1000 K). Each line comes from an equilibrium constant, for example

\mathrm{NiS} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{NiO} + \mathrm{SO_2}: \quad \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} = \log K + \tfrac{3}{2}\log p_{\mathrm{O_2}}\ (\text{slope } 3/2)
\mathrm{NiO} + \mathrm{SO_2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{NiSO_4}: \quad \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} = -\log K - \tfrac{1}{2}\log p_{\mathrm{O_2}}\ (\text{slope } -1/2)

Uses.

  1. Predicts the roast product for a given gas composition and temperature, so conditions can be set for an oxide (dead roast before reduction), a sulphate (sulphating roast before leaching) or a partial roast.
  2. Selective roasting: superimposed diagrams of two metals (Cu-S-O and Fe-S-O) show where Cu forms a soluble sulphate while Fe forms insoluble \mathrm{Fe_2O_3}.
  3. Shows whether the metal itself can form directly (the metal field).

Limitations.

  1. Equilibrium only: gives no rates; real products depend on kinetics (oxide-layer diffusion) and may differ.
  2. Assumes pure condensed phases at unit activity; ignores solid solutions, mattes, liquids and compounds such as ferrites (\mathrm{ZnFe_2O_4}) and basic sulphates.
  3. One temperature per diagram; real roasters have temperature gradients.
  4. Only as accurate as the thermodynamic data.
pts: Defines it: isothermal plot of \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} showing the area in which each condensed phase (metal, sulphide, oxide, sulphate) is stable
Plotted from thermodynamic data: lines from equilibrium constants, slopes from stoichiometry (for example 3/2 for sulphide/oxide, -1/2 for oxide/sulphate)
Use: choosing roasting conditions (temperature, gas) to obtain the desired product: oxide, sulphate or partial roast
Use: selective roasting by superimposing diagrams of two metals, or predicting direct metal formation
Limitation: equilibrium only, no kinetics, so actual products may differ
Limitation: pure phases at unit activity assumed; solid solutions, mattes, ferrites and complex compounds ignored
Limitation: one temperature per diagram, or depends on data accuracy
1a.watch:
• Name the axes: \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} at constant temperature. Some texts use \log p_{\mathrm{S_2}} instead; it is the same diagram in other coordinates.
  • On the slide the Ni/NiO line lies near \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} = -15.4; from \Delta G^\circ = -471\,200 + 172T J for 2\mathrm{Ni} + \mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{NiO} it is -15.6 at 1000 K, the same within reading error.
  • On the slide's diagram the usual roaster gas (a few % \mathrm{O_2}, about 10% \mathrm{SO_2}) plots in the \mathrm{NiSO_4} field at 1000 K, not far above the NiO line; a higher temperature or less \mathrm{SO_2} is needed for a dead roast to NiO.

1b.html:
In fluidised-bed roasting the ore particles are roasted while suspended in an upward stream of air. Air from a wind box passes through a grid (distributor) under a bed of fine concentrate; the feed enters the bed, the roasted calcine overflows, and the hot gases with \mathrm{SO_2} and fines leave at the top for the cyclones. A water spray controls the temperature, and auxiliary fuel is used at start-up. As the gas velocity is raised, the bed passes through these stages:

  1. Fixed bed: at a very low flow the gas permeates the porous bed without disturbing the particles; the pressure drop is proportional to the flow rate.
  2. Expanded bed (AB): as the velocity increases the bed loosens and expands upward; the pressure drop still depends on the velocity.
  3. Lifting point (BC): the pressure drop approaches the weight of the bed per unit area, with a small peak, and the particles are just lifted at the minimum fluidisation velocity.
  4. Fluidised bed (C onward): the pressure drop stays constant, independent of velocity; extra gas passes as bubbles and the bed flows like a liquid. The roaster operates here: every particle is surrounded by gas, mixing is intense, and the temperature is uniform, so the roast is fast and even.
  5. Entrainment: above the particles' terminal velocity they are carried out of the bed (pneumatic transport) and the pressure drop falls; the gas velocity is kept below this.
pts: Principle: particles roasted while suspended in an upward air stream blown through a grid, with feed into the bed and calcine overflow
Equipment detail: water spray or auxiliary fuel for temperature, gases and fines to cyclones
Stage 1, fixed bed: gas permeates without disturbing the particles; pressure drop proportional to flow rate
Stage 2, expanded bed: the bed expands upward and the pressure drop depends on velocity (AB)
Stage 3, lifting point at the minimum fluidisation velocity, pressure drop reaching the bed weight per unit area (BC)
Stage 4, fluidised bed: pressure drop independent of velocity, bed flows like a liquid; the operating stage with uniform temperature and good contact
Stage 5, entrainment or pneumatic transport above the terminal velocity; the gas velocity is kept below it
1b.watch:
• The slides describe four stages; the fifth, entrainment, is the textbook end of the curve. Some texts split stage 4 into smooth and bubbling beds instead; either set of five earns the marks if each is described.
  • At C it is the pressure drop that becomes independent of velocity (it equals the bed weight per unit area); the bed itself still swells a little as bubbles pass.

1c.html:
Principle. A narrow molten zone is moved slowly along a partly purified solid bar. Impurities that lower the melting point collect in the liquid, travel with the zone to the far end, and that end is cut off.

From the phase diagram. The liquidus and the solidus both fall from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus more steeply, so at every temperature the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium with it:

k = \frac{C_S}{C_L} < 1

A melt of composition X (C_0) starts to freeze at L_1 and deposits solid S_1 with only kC_0.

Effect of the moving zone. Purer solid freezes at the back of the zone; the rejected impurity stays in the zone, which melts fresh charge at its front, so the impurity is carried forward. The first solid holds kC_0, the impurity content rises along the bar, and the last zone length freezes impure and is cropped.

Multiple passes in the same direction: the more passes, the purer the starting end. For k = 0.3 the start holds 0.3C_0 after one pass and about 0.01C_0 after five.

Conditions. k far from 1 and slow zone travel. Impurities with k > 1 move the other way, to the starting end. The method gives ultra-pure Si, Ge and Ga.
pts: Principle: a narrow molten zone moved slowly along a solid bar sweeps the impurities into the liquid and to one end, which is cut off
Phase diagram: temperature against impurity concentration, liquidus and solidus falling from T_m of the pure metal, three fields labelled, tie lines S_1L_1 and S_2L_2
States from the diagram that the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium, k = C_S/C_L < 1 (S_1 purer than L_1)
The purer solid freezes at the back of the zone and the rejected impurity is carried forward; the first solid holds kC_0 and the impure last part is cropped
Multiple passes in the same direction raise the purity at the starting end
A condition or use: k far from 1, slow zone travel, impurities with k > 1 move to the starting end, or products such as Si, Ge, Ga
1c.sketch:
• Axes: temperature (vertical) against impurity (solute) concentration (horizontal).
  • Liquidus and solidus both falling from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus below and steeper.
  • Fields labelled Liquid, Solid + Liquid, Solid.
  • Vertical line X for the melt C_0; tie line S_1 L_1 where freezing starts and S_2 L_2 where it ends.
  • k = C_S/C_L < 1 written on the diagram.
1c.watch:
• The phase diagram carries the marks for "principles": label the axes, both lines and the tie line, and say which composition is the solid.
  • Do not say the impurity "evaporates" or is "removed" in the zone: it is only redistributed along the bar, and the impure end must be cut off.
  • Fast zone travel lets the rejected impurity build up ahead of the freezing front, so the effective k moves towards 1 and each pass removes much less impurity.
  • Extra depth: silicon is refined by the floating-zone method (no container) because molten Si reacts with crucible materials and picks up oxygen and other contamination; after many passes the profile reaches a limiting (ultimate) distribution, set by k and the zone length.

2a.html:
A potential/pH (Pourbaix) diagram shows the predominant species of a metal at equilibrium at each reduction potential E and pH, for a chosen metal-ion activity (10^{-3} for leaching). Its lines divide it into domains of metal, oxide and soluble ions, and the two water stability lines (\mathrm{H_2} and \mathrm{O_2}) are drawn on it.

Importance in leaching.

  1. Choice of conditions. It shows whether a mineral can dissolve in the system at all, and over what pH and E its ion stays in solution. The pH is then set with acid or alkali, and E with an oxidant, a reductant or an applied potential. If no soluble species forms, another reagent system is examined.
  2. Zinc example. Zn and ZnO dissolve as \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} below pH about 6.9 and as \mathrm{ZnO_2^{2-}} above about 13.4; the farther from the \mathrm{ZnO/Zn^{2+}} line, the better the leach.
  3. Need for an oxidant. Against the water lines: Zn (-0.76 V) dissolves in deaerated acid with \mathrm{H_2} evolution; Cu (+0.34 V) needs \mathrm{O_2} (E_{\mathrm{cell}} = +0.89 V) or \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}; for Au (+1.50 V) even \mathrm{O_2} fails (E_{\mathrm{cell}} = -0.27 V), so cyanide must complex it.

Conclusion. The diagrams fix reagent, pH and oxidant from thermodynamics; the rate must still be found by experiment.
pts: Shows the predominant (stable) species at each E and pH, as domains for a chosen ion activity (about 10^{-3}), with the water stability lines drawn on
Used to select leaching conditions: whether and where the ion is stable, then pH set by acid or alkali and E by an oxidant, reductant or applied potential
Zn example: dissolves as \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} below pH about 6.9 or as zincate above about 13.4, more efficiently farther from the boundary
Water-line comparison: Zn dissolves by \mathrm{H^+} reduction, Cu needs \mathrm{O_2} or another oxidant, Au needs a complexing agent such as cyanide
Concludes that they predict thermodynamic feasibility only; the rate must be found by experiment
2a.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 12, 18-30; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 7, 10-11
2a.watch:
• Quote the pH limits for the activity used (book Figure 5.3 is for 10^{-3}); at a lower activity the dissolution domains widen.
  • The lines are not absolute limits: they mark where one species holds most of the metal.
  • The slides call the upper water line "oxygen reduction" (the cathodic reaction that leaching uses); in the diagram the same line marks \mathrm{O_2} evolution when crossed upwards.

2b.html:
The two situations (sketches)

In both, the reagent R must reach the mineral surface and the dissolved metal species M and other products P must move away into the solution. A liquid boundary layer at the surface carries the concentration gradients.

(a) The mineral dissolves completely. No solid product forms and the surface simply recedes, for example CuO in dilute \mathrm{H_2SO_4}. R falls from its bulk value [R]_B to [R]_S at the surface; M and P fall from [M]_S, [P]_S to [M]_B, [P]_B.

(b) The mineral decomposes and dissolves only in part. A new solid residue forms on the mineral, for example \mathrm{CaWO_4 + CO_3^{2-} \rightarrow CaCO_3 + WO_4^{2-}}. Leaching continues only if this residue is porous. Interface I is mineral/residue and interface II is residue/solution.

Kinetic steps

Case (a), three steps:

  1. Diffusion of R from the bulk solution to the mineral-solution interface.
  2. Reaction of R with the mineral surface, forming a soluble metal species.
  3. Diffusion of M (or P) away from the interface into the bulk.

Case (b), five steps (the more general case):

  1. Diffusion of R from the bulk to the residue-solution interface II.
  2. Diffusion of R through the porous product layer.
  3. Reaction of R with the mineral at interface I.
  4. Outward diffusion of M and P through the porous layer.
  5. Diffusion of M and P from interface II into the bulk.

Without a residue, steps 2 and 4 vanish and (b) reduces to (a). The slowest step (or steps) sets the rate, so it must be identified before choosing a remedy.

Accelerating the leaching

  • Film diffusion control (steps 1, 5): stir or agitate the pulp. This thins the boundary layer and steepens the gradients, so the rate rises with stirring speed until the layer reaches a limiting thickness. Diffusion-limited leaching uses high-speed propeller or turbine agitators. A stronger bulk reagent concentration also raises the driving force.
  • Chemical reaction control (step 3): agitation has no effect. Raise the temperature, since the activation energy is high, 10-25 kcal/mol (42-105 kJ/mol); raise the reagent concentration (the effect depends on the reaction order); supply more oxidant, for example oxygen under pressure in an autoclave.
  • Pore diffusion control (steps 2, 4): stirring does not reach inside the residue; finer grinding shortens the path, and roasting can make the product porous.
  • For every case: finer grinding exposes more surface (10 mm to 0.1 mm gives 100 times the area), and higher temperature speeds up all steps; diffusion, with an activation energy of 5 kcal/mol (21 kJ/mol) or less, gains least.
pts: Sketch (a): mineral and solution with [R] falling from [R]_B to [R]_S and [M], [P] falling from the surface to bulk values, labelled
Sketch (b): porous residue between mineral and solution with interfaces I and II and the R, M, P profiles labelled with subscripts I and II
Explains situation (a): complete dissolution, no solid product, the surface recedes, with an example (CuO in dilute acid)
Explains situation (b): partial dissolution leaving a solid residue that must be porous for leaching to continue, with an example (\mathrm{CaWO_4} in carbonate)
Case (a) steps: reagent diffusion to the surface, surface reaction to a soluble species, diffusion of products away
Case (b) five steps, including diffusion of R through the porous layer, reaction at interface I and outward diffusion of M and P through the layer
States that the slowest step controls the rate and must be identified first
Film diffusion (steps 1, 5): stirring or agitation thins the boundary layer, the rate rising to a plateau; high-speed agitators for diffusion-limited leaching
Reaction control (step 3): agitation has no effect; raise temperature (activation energy 10-25 kcal/mol, 42-105 kJ/mol) or reagent concentration or oxidant pressure
Finer grinding raises the surface area (and shortens the pore path), and stirring does not help pore diffusion
Higher temperature accelerates every step, diffusion least (5 kcal/mol, 21 kJ/mol, or less)
2b.sketch:
• (a) Mineral (hatched) beside the solution; curves of [R] rising from [R]_S at the surface to [R]_B, and of [M], [P] falling from [M]_S, [P]_S to [M]_B, [P]_B.
  • (b) A porous residue layer between mineral and solution, interfaces I and II marked; [R] rising from [R]_I through [R]_{II} to the bulk, [M] and [P] falling from [M]_I, [P]_I through [M]_{II}, [P]_{II}.
  • Arrows numbering the kinetic steps in each case.
2b.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 13-17; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 4, 6, 13-15
2b.watch:
• Slide numbering: "step 1 or step 5" and "step 3" refer to case (b). In case (a) the reaction is the second of three steps.
  • A rate that stops rising with stirring is not proof of reaction control: diffusion through a limiting boundary layer can remain rate-controlling, and only the activation energy then tells them apart.
  • At high temperature diffusion control becomes more likely, because the reaction rate grows faster with temperature than the diffusion rate.

3a.fix: Slide 10 of the hydrometallurgy deck writes the cyanidation reaction as 4\mathrm{Au} + 8\mathrm{NaCN} + \mathrm{O_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} = 4\mathrm{NaAu(CN)_2} + \mathrm{NaOH}. This is unbalanced (8 Na, 4 O and 4 H on the left). The product side needs 4\,\mathrm{NaOH}, as the course book writes it on pages 12-13.
3a.html:
A Pachuca vat is a vessel for agitation (slime) leaching: finely ground ore or concentrate, about 200 μm, is leached as a pulp that is kept moving to speed up the reaction.

Construction. A tall cylindrical tank, typically about 4 m in diameter and 15 m high, with a conical bottom, made of wood or rubber-lined steel. A central pipe, coaxial with the tank and open at both ends, runs from near the apex of the cone to just below the pulp surface. Compressed air enters at the lower end of this pipe.

How leaching is accomplished.

  1. Pulp (ore plus leach solution) is fed in at the top.
  2. Air lift: the air bubbles in the central pipe make the pulp there less dense than the pulp around it. The pressure of the denser surrounding pulp therefore pushes the aerated pulp up the pipe, and it overflows at the top.
  3. The pulp flows down the annulus between pipe and wall; the conical bottom guides the solids back to the foot of the pipe, so they do not settle and the entire charge circulates.
  4. Aeration: where the reaction consumes oxygen, the same air supplies it, for example gold cyanidation:
4\mathrm{Au} + 8\mathrm{NaCN} + \mathrm{O_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NaAu(CN)_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH}
  1. Heating: live steam can be injected with the air, giving pulp temperatures up to about 60-70°C.
  2. The leached pulp is discharged through the outlet to solid-liquid separation (thickening, filtration), which gives the pregnant liquor.

Merits. The vat is very simple and has no moving parts to go out of order, so maintenance is low; Pachucas are widely used in slime leaching, for example of gold ores.
pts: Sketch: tall cylindrical tank with a conical bottom and a central pipe open at both ends, labelled
Sketch: compressed air entering at the foot of the pipe, circulation arrows (up the pipe, down the annulus), pulp inlet and outlet
Agitation (slime) leaching of finely ground pulp (about 200 μm); about 4 m diameter by 15 m high, wood or rubber-lined steel
Air-lift principle: bubbles lower the pulp density in the pipe, so the denser surrounding pulp pushes it up and it overflows
The whole charge circulates down the annulus, the cone returning the solids to the pipe so they stay suspended
Agitation also aerates the pulp for oxygen-consuming reactions, such as gold cyanidation (balanced equation)
Live steam injected with the air heats the pulp to about 60-70°C
No moving parts, simple and low maintenance; widely used in slime leaching
Pulp fed at the top and the leached pulp discharged to solid-liquid separation
3a.sketch:
• Tall cylindrical tank with a conical bottom; central pipe open at both ends.
  • Compressed air (and steam) inlet at the foot of the central pipe.
  • Circulation arrows: up the pipe, overflow at the top, down the annulus, back into the pipe at the cone.
  • Pulp inlet at the top and pulp outlet; tank material and size noted.
3a.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 42-43; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 12-13, 18
3a.watch:
• Agitation in a Pachuca is by air, not by an impeller; do not draw a stirrer.
  • Pachuca vats suit fine pulps; coarse ore that drains freely is leached by percolation instead.
  • The slides print the cyanidation product as "NaOH"; the balanced equation needs 4\,\mathrm{NaOH}.

3b.fix: • The course book (p 34) prints E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.337 - (-440) and \Delta G^\circ = \sim 149.9 kJ/mol: the iron potential is -0.440 V and \Delta G^\circ is negative, -149.9 kJ per mol Fe. Its ratio 4\times10^{-27} follows from a cell of 0.78 V; 0.777 V gives 5\times10^{-27} (either is acceptable).
3b.html:
The metal is won from a clear leach liquor by cementation (contact reduction), gaseous reduction or electrolysis. Cementation is reduction by another metal: a less noble metal (more negative electrode potential) is added, dissolves, and the more noble metal precipitates on its surface.

Principle

For \mathrm{M^{z+} + ze^- = M}, with unit activity of the pure metal,

E = E^\circ + \frac{RT}{zF}\ln a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}}

The metal with the more negative potential passes into solution and displaces the metal of more positive potential. The series is for 25 C and unit activity, so real concentrations can change the order for metals of close potential.

Mechanism (a corrosion cell)

The precipitant corrodes anodically, and reduction of the noble ion is the cathodic reaction:

\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}\qquad \mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}

At first small potential differences on the surface give local cells and the rate is low. Dissolved oxygen (\mathrm{O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 2H_2O}) is reduced preferentially and wastes precipitant, so oxygen is excluded. Once some metal has deposited, it forms a galvanic cell with the precipitant, the whole exposed surface becomes anodic and the rate rises.

Example: copper on scrap iron

\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{CuSO_4 + Fe \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu}\\ &E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.337 - (-0.440) = 0.777\ \mathrm{V},\qquad \Delta G^\circ = -2(96485)(0.777) \approx -150\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\\ &a_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}}/a_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}} \approx 5\times10^{-27}\ \text{at equilibrium} \end{aligned}

So practically all copper can be removed. The liquor runs through long troughs (launders) of scrap steel. Copper forms a curd-like precipitate contaminated with iron residues that must be fire-refined. Iron needed in theory is 55.85/63.55 = 0.88 kg per kg Cu, but acid and ferric ions also consume it:

\mathrm{Fe + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + H_2}\qquad \mathrm{Fe + Fe_2(SO_4)_3 \rightarrow 3FeSO_4}

Other uses

  • Gold and silver: zinc dust added to a clarified, de-aerated cyanide solution: \mathrm{2[Au(CN)_2]^- + Zn \rightarrow 2Au + [Zn(CN)_4]^{2-}}.
  • Purification: zinc dust removes Cu and Cd from zinc sulphate electrolyte (\mathrm{Cd^{2+} + Zn \rightarrow Cd + Zn^{2+}}).

The process is simple and cheap and works on dilute solutions, but the product is impure and the precipitant is consumed. It goes faster with a large precipitant area (scrap, dust), good flow past the surface and no oxygen.
pts: Defines cementation: reduction of noble metal ions by a less noble metal that dissolves, the metal depositing on its surface; one of the recovery methods (with gaseous reduction, electrolysis)
Principle: the metal with the more negative reduction potential dissolves and displaces the more positive one; E = E^\circ + (RT/zF)\ln a
The series holds at 25 C and unit activity; concentrations can change the order

Mechanism: precipitant anodic (\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}), noble ion reduced at the cathode (\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}); local cells first, then a galvanic cell with the deposit
Dissolved oxygen is reduced preferentially and wastes precipitant, so it is excluded
Cu/Fe numbers: cell about 0.78 V, \Delta G^\circ about -150 kJ/mol, equilibrium ratio of order 10^{-27}, so removal is nearly complete
Copper practice: liquor through troughs of scrap iron, \mathrm{CuSO_4 + Fe \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu}, curd-like impure cement copper that is fire-refined
Iron consumption: 0.88 kg Fe per kg Cu in theory, more because acid (and ferric ions) also dissolve iron
Gold or silver with zinc dust from de-aerated cyanide solution, with a balanced equation (or zinc dust purification of zinc electrolyte)
Merits and limits or rate factors: simple, cheap, dilute solutions; impure product, precipitant consumed; area, flow, no oxygen

3b.watch:
• No sketch is asked, so none is credited; the figure redraws the slide's corrosion cell.
  • Use one sign convention. With reduction potentials the metal with the more negative potential dissolves; the book's Table 5.1 lists oxidation potentials (signs reversed), which is why its text says "more positive".
  • Gold cementation needs the solution clarified and de-aerated; dissolved oxygen would redissolve gold in cyanide and waste zinc.
  • The same question was set in 2013-14 (3b).

4a.html:
An electrolyte for metal extraction or refining should:

  1. High ionic conductivity, so the IR drop and energy are low.
  2. High solubility of the metal salt, giving a high metal-ion concentration (cryolite dissolves \mathrm{Al_2O_3}).
  3. Stability: only the wanted metal is discharged; other constituents have higher decomposition voltages and do not volatilise or hydrolyse.
  4. No attack on the deposit, electrodes or cell lining; a dense, adherent deposit.
  5. Cheap, easily purified and regenerated. A fused-salt bath also needs a low melting point and a density different from the metal.
pts: High electrical (ionic) conductivity, to keep the voltage and energy low
High solubility of the metal compound, giving an adequate metal-ion concentration
Chemical and electrochemical stability: no constituent other than the metal is discharged, no volatilisation or hydrolysis
No chemical attack on the deposit, electrodes or cell materials (a sound deposit results)
Cheap, easily purified and regenerated, or (fused salt) low melting point and a density different from the metal
4a.watch:
• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • "List" asks for short points; one line per condition is enough for 5 marks.
  • The same question appears in 2013-14 Q4a (with electrowinning against electrorefining) and 2015-16 Q4a.

4b.html:
Relative activity. The electrochemical series ranks metals by their standard reduction potential against the hydrogen electrode (0 V). The more negative E^\circ, the more reactive the metal and the harder its ion is to reduce: Au +1.50, Ag +0.80, Cu +0.34, H 0.00, Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Zn -0.76, Mn -1.18, Al -1.66, Mg -2.37, Na -2.71 V.

Cathode competition. In water the metal ion competes with hydrogen, and the reaction with the more positive deposition potential wins:

E_{\mathrm{M}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{M}} + \frac{0.0592}{z}\log a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}} - \eta_{\mathrm{M}}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}} = -0.0592\,\mathrm{pH} - \eta_{\mathrm{H}}

The metal deposits when E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}}; \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is the hydrogen overvoltage on the cathode surface.

1. Metals nobler than hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au). E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}} even in strong acid and at low metal activity, so they deposit readily. Hydrogen appears mainly when the current density approaches the limiting current. Copper is won from about 150-180 g/L \mathrm{H_2SO_4} at 85-95 % current efficiency.

2. Less noble metals with a high hydrogen overvoltage (Zn, Cd, Pb, Sn, Mn). By equilibrium hydrogen should evolve first, but on these metals \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is about 0.7-1 V (against below 0.1 V on Pt), which pushes E_{\mathrm{H}} below E_{\mathrm{M}}. Zinc is won at 400-600 A/m^2, 35-40 ^\circC, on Al cathodes, at about 90 % efficiency, but only from a deeply purified electrolyte: Co, Ni, Sb, Ge lower \eta_{\mathrm{H}} and re-dissolve the zinc. Mn (-1.18 V) needs a near-neutral ammonium sulphate electrolyte and gives only about 60-70 %.

3. Less noble metals with a low hydrogen overvoltage (Fe, Ni, Co). They need a weakly acid (pH about 2-4), warm electrolyte, often with diaphragms, and give lower efficiency.

4. Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na, Ca, Li, Ti). E^\circ lies below about -1.6 V: no attainable overvoltage stops hydrogen evolution, the current goes to \mathrm{H_2}, and any metal formed reacts with water:

\mathrm{2Al + 6H_2O \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3H_2}

Raising the pH does not help, because the hydroxide precipitates first.

Conclusion. Whether a metal can be electrowon from water is set by its potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration. The most reactive metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis: Al from cryolite-alumina, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl.
pts: Explains the electrochemical series: metals ranked by E^\circ against hydrogen (0 V), more negative means more reactive, with values
At the cathode the reaction with the more positive deposition potential occurs first; metal ion and \mathrm{H^+} compete (Nernst forms for both)
Nobler metals (Cu, Ag, Au) deposit readily even from strong acid; hydrogen mainly near the limiting current
Less noble metals: thermodynamically hydrogen should be discharged first
Hydrogen overvoltage (high on Zn, Pb, Hg; low on Pt) moves the hydrogen potential below that of the metal, so Zn, Cd, Pb, Mn can deposit
Operating conditions for zinc (high current density, low temperature, pure electrolyte free of Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) and about 90 % efficiency
Fe, Ni, Co with low overvoltage need pH control and give lower efficiency
Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na; E^\circ below about -1.6 V): hydrogen evolves instead and the metal would react with water (balanced equation)
Concludes that such metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis, with examples (Hall-Heroult Al, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl)
States the overall criterion: potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration

• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • A list of the series alone earns little; the marks are for the hydrogen competition and the overvoltage argument.

4c.html:
Harmful impurities

  1. Lower the conductivity (in solid solution): P, Fe, Si, As, Sb, Sn, Ni, Co. Only 0.015-0.04 % P gives about 85 % IACS, against about 101 % for tough-pitch copper.
  2. Spoil drawing and annealing: Bi, Pb (grain-boundary embrittlement), Se, Te, S; Bi harms at a few ppm.

Elimination during electrorefining

Crude anodes (about 99.5 % Cu) dissolve in \mathrm{CuSO_4}-\mathrm{H_2SO_4} at about 60 ^\circC and 0.3 V, and copper plates on the cathode (\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}). The low voltage separates impurities by potential:

  • Au, Ag, Pt metals (nobler) do not dissolve and go to the anode slime.
  • Se, Te (as selenides and tellurides), Pb (as \mathrm{PbSO_4}) and Sn also report to the slime.
  • Ni, Fe, Zn, Co (baser) dissolve and stay in solution; a bleed removes them.
  • As, Sb, Bi (close to Cu) may co-deposit or form floating slime; they are kept low by the bleed and liberator cells.

Addition agents (glue, thiourea) and filtered electrolyte give a dense cathode of about 99.99 % Cu.
pts: Impurities that lower conductivity (P, Fe, Si, As, Sb, Sn, Ni), with an example of the effect
Impurities that spoil workability (Bi, Pb, Se, Te, S) at ppm level
Refining set-up and principle: crude anode dissolves, Cu plates, low voltage separates impurities by potential
Nobler metals (Au, Ag, Pt) to the anode slime
Se, Te, Pb, Sn to the slime as insoluble compounds
Base metals (Ni, Fe, Zn, Co) stay in solution, removed by bleeding
As, Sb, Bi controlled by bleed or liberator cells because they can co-deposit

5a.html:
1. Collection. Obsolete scrap comes from many scattered sources, so collection is highly labour intensive and has held back supply. Bringing e-waste and spent batteries back to the smelter ("reverse logistics") is a major challenge.
  2. Sorting. Scrap arrives as mixed alloys and materials. It must be sorted by composition so that alloys can be remelted as alloys (brass as brass), again a labour-intensive step.
  3. Uncertain supply and price. Obsolete scrap depends on product lifetime (car 10-12 years, lead-acid battery 2-4 years), and scrap prices fluctuate, which can make a recovery process uneconomic.
  4. Tramp elements. Cu from wiring and Sn from tinplate dissolve in steel and cannot be refined out, because they are nobler than Fe. They build up with each cycle and cause hot shortness, so the metal must be diluted with primary metal or down-cycled to rebar.
  5. Complexity: a smartphone holds over 60 elements in traces, so separation is costly.
  6. Hazards: Hg, Cd and flame retardants need expensive off-gas treatment.
pts: Collection: scattered sources make it labour intensive, which limits supply; reverse logistics for e-waste and batteries
Sorting by composition is needed so alloys are recycled as alloys (brass as brass), and is labour intensive
Uncertain supply and fluctuating price of obsolete scrap, which depends on product lifetime (car 10-12 years, battery 2-4 years)
Tramp elements Cu and Sn in steel cannot be removed (nobler than Fe), build up and cause hot shortness, forcing dilution or down-cycling
Complexity of modern products (smartphone with over 60 elements)
Hazardous components (Hg, Cd, flame retardants) needing off-gas treatment

  • If remedies are also asked: better collection and sorting, standard scrap grades, and dilution with primary metal.

5b.html:
Mineral: a naturally occurring, crystalline, mostly inorganic compound of nearly fixed composition and definite properties, for example galena (PbS) or chalcopyrite (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}).

Ore: a natural aggregate of value minerals and gangue from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently, for example bauxite for aluminium.

BasisMineralOre
Natureone specific compoundvalue minerals plus gangue
Deciding testcomposition and structuremetal extracted at a profit
Constancyfixed: galena is always galenachanges with price and technology
Relationnot every mineral is an oreevery ore is made of minerals
Exampleclay (about 20% Al)bauxite, the Al ore
pts: Defines a mineral as a natural crystalline compound of nearly fixed composition, with an example
Defines an ore as an aggregate of value minerals and gangue from which a metal is extracted profitably, with an example
Gives at least two differences (one compound against an aggregate, chemical against economic test, not every mineral is an ore)
Notes that ore status changes with price and technology, or gives a contrasting pair such as clay and bauxite

5b.watch:
• Same question as 2015-16 Q11(b). The contrast that earns the marks is "a mineral is always the same compound; an ore is a mineral deposit that pays".
  • Clay holds about 20% Al but is not an Al ore, because the Al is locked in a silicate that is costly to break down.

5c.html:
Definition. Ore dressing is the physical (and sometimes limited chemical) treatment of ore that separates the value minerals from the gangue, giving a concentrate and tailings that can be treated economically for metal extraction. No metal is produced.

Importance. Mined ore arrives in lumps of 1200-1500 mm, an intimate mixture of value and gangue grains. Dressing:

  • cuts the tonnage, so freight and extraction cost (fuel, flux, energy) fall;
  • reduces slag and so the metal lost in it;
  • makes lean ores workable (0.5% Cu rock is processed today), expanding reserves;
  • splits complex Cu-Pb-Zn ores into separate concentrates (selective beneficiation).

Steps.

  1. Comminution: crushing (jaw, gyratory, cone crushers) then grinding (rod and ball mills) until the particle size approaches the grain size, so that most particles are liberated (one phase) rather than composite. Over-grinding is avoided because very fine particles separate poorly.
  2. Sizing: screening for coarse sizes and classification (by settling velocity in water or air) for fine sizes; oversize returns to the mill in closed circuit.
  3. Concentration (particle selection): by specific gravity (jigs, tables, heavy media), magnetic susceptibility (magnetic separation), electrical conductivity (electrostatic separation) or surface wettability (froth flotation). Products: concentrate, middlings, tailings.
  4. Dewatering: thickening, filtration and drying of the concentrate before shipping or smelting.
pts: Defines ore dressing as separation of value minerals from gangue, mainly by physical methods, giving a concentrate and tailings, without producing metal
Lists at least three points of importance: lower freight and extraction cost from reduced tonnage, less metal lost in slag, lean ores made workable (0.5% Cu), separate concentrates from complex ores
Comminution: crushing and grinding to liberate the value mineral, with liberated against composite particles and no over-grinding
Sizing: screening and classification by settling velocity, oversize returned in closed circuit
Concentration methods matched to the property used: density, magnetism, conductivity, wettability; products concentrate, middlings and tailings
Dewatering: thickening, filtration and drying
Gives the four steps in order (comminution, sizing, concentration, dewatering), in words or as a flowsheet with the closed-circuit recycle
5c.sketch:
• Flowsheet boxes in sequence: run-of-mine ore, crushing, grinding, sizing (screen or classifier), concentration, dewatering (thickener and filter), concentrate to the smelter.
  • A recycle arrow from the sizing box back to grinding, labelled "oversize, closed circuit".
  • From the concentration box, three outputs labelled concentrate, middlings (back to grinding) and tailings (to the dump).
  • Beside the comminution boxes, a small drawing of one ore lump with dark value grains in light gangue, broken into liberated and composite particles.

5c.watch:
• The book names four principal operations: comminution, sizing, particle selection (concentration) and dewatering. Give all four, in order.
  • Liberation is the reason for grinding: the degree of liberation is the percentage of a mineral present as free particles out of its total (free plus locked).
  • "List the importance" wants short points; save the words for "discuss the steps", which carries most of the marks.

5d.html:
Commercial size reduction applies stress in three ways, and each gives a different product size:

  1. Slow compression (jaw, gyratory and smooth roll crushers). Stress is set up throughout the particle and raised gradually until the resolved tensile and shear stresses are just enough to propagate the pre-existing cracks. The largest cracks run first, so fracture occurs at only a few places: a few large fragments, relatively large compared with the original particle, in a narrow size range.
  2. Fast compression or impact (hammer, stamp, impact at the toe of a ball mill). The rapid loading extends the existing cracks and forms new ones, so the particle shatters into many fragments much smaller than the original, over a wide size range.
  3. Abrasion (rubbing against neighbouring particles or hard surfaces, as in zones A and B of a tumbling mill). High shear stresses act only near the surface, so fracture is localised at the surface. The distribution is bimodal: one mode close to the original size (the worn core) and one at very small sizes (the fines).

So the faster and more localised the stress, the finer the product: crushers working by slow compression make coarse products, mills working by impact and abrasion make fines.
pts: Names the three techniques: slow compression, fast compression (impact) and abrasion
Slow compression: stress raised gradually until pre-existing (largest) cracks propagate, fracture at a few places, so a few large fragments close to the original size
Fast compression: existing cracks extended and new cracks formed, so many fragments much smaller than the original over a wide range
Abrasion: high shear near the surface, fracture localised at the surface, so a bimodal distribution (one mode near the original size, one very fine)
Sketch of the fragments or the size distributions for the three techniques
Links each technique to machines (crushers by slow compression, impact in hammer or ball mills, abrasion in tumbling mills) and concludes which gives the finest product
5d.src: Size reduction, slides 7, 9, 27, 29; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 2-3, 14
5d.watch:
• "Relate" asks for the link: for each technique say what happens to the cracks and what size distribution results; a list of the three names earns little.
  • Abrasion does not simply give "fine" particles: it leaves the core nearly at its original size, hence the two modes.

Crushing elements fixed relative to one another in crushers (set adjustment needed) against free media held apart only by the ore in mills (no set adjustment)

6a.watch:
• The three differences the course text stresses are size restriction, how the energy is applied and fixed against free crushing elements; give these first.
  • Roll crushers also need adjustment for set; only the mills (and stamps) do not.

6b.fix: • Slide 10 says the large lumps in the upper part of the jaws are broken "by impact force" and only the small ones lower down by compression. A jaw crusher breaks every lump by compression (slide 9 says so itself): the swing jaw moves slowly and least near the pivot at the top, so the large lumps there are nipped and squeezed, not struck.
6b.html:
Working (Blake jaw crusher). Feed enters between two jaws set in a V open at the top. The fixed jaw is nearly vertical; the swing jaw, pivoted at the top, makes 20 to 30° with it. An eccentric on the flywheel shaft drives a pitman up and down, which straightens and bends two toggle plates and so moves the bottom of the swing jaw towards the fixed jaw and back, 250 to 400 times per minute. Lumps caught between the upper parts of the jaws are broken by compression, drop into the narrower space below and are re-crushed at the next closing, until they pass the throat. Flywheels even out this intermittent load.

Important characteristics.

  1. Size: quoted as gape × jaw width; a 66 × 84 in crusher takes rock under 66 in.
  2. Set and stroke: the set (average, often minimum, throat opening) fixes the product size; the stroke (throw) is the difference between the open and closed throat openings, short for brittle rock (quartz) and long for tough rock that deforms.
  3. Reduction ratio = gape / set; the actual value is lower, since the largest feed lumps are smaller than the gape.
  4. Capacity (t/h of product) rises with speed and falls as the reduction ratio rises; power is proportional to the crushing done.
  5. No choking: the Blake jaw moves most at the bottom of the V.
  6. Wear: manganese steel liners; wear enlarges the set, so it must be adjusted often.
pts: Construction: nearly vertical fixed jaw and a swing jaw pivoted at the top, forming a V at 20 to 30°
Drive: eccentric, pitman and toggles move the bottom of the swing jaw 250 to 400 times per minute; flywheels even out the intermittent load
Action: lumps nipped and broken by compression near the top, fall into the narrower space and are re-crushed until they pass the throat
Size quoted as gape × width (66 × 84 in), the gape fixing the largest lump accepted
Set (throat opening, fixes product size) and stroke or throw (short for brittle, long for tough rock) defined
Reduction ratio = gape / set, the actual value lower than calculated
Capacity rises with speed and falls with reduction ratio, or the Blake jaw moves most at the bottom so it does not choke
Manganese steel liners whose wear enlarges the set, so the set must be adjusted

  • Eccentric, pitman and toggles; the closed position of the swing jaw dashed.
  • Gape at the mouth, set at the throat and the stroke between the open and closed positions.

6b.watch:
• The jaw crusher breaks by slow compression, not by impact: the jaw near the pivot hardly moves.
  • Do not confuse the Blake crusher (pivot at the top, greatest motion at the bottom, no choking) with the Dodge crusher (pivot at the bottom, little oversize but many fines, tends to choke).
  • Extra depth: slide 8 quotes feed sizes of 1500 to 40 mm, products of 50 to 5 mm and rock up to about 320 MPa compressive strength.

6c.html:
A smooth roll crusher breaks particles by compression alone, and only those it can nip: with roll radius R, gap d and particle radius r,

\cos\alpha = \frac{R + d/2}{R + r},\qquad \text{nipped if } \tan\alpha \le \mu

with an angle of nip 2\alpha of about 32°. So 1 m rolls set 12.5 mm apart take lumps of only about 53 mm, a reduction ratio near 4.

Advantages of toothed (corrugated or breaker-bar) rolls:

  1. No nip limit: the teeth grip and draw in the lumps, so they reduce much larger particles for a given roll size (heavy double-roll crushers take feed up to about 500 mm).
  2. Compression, impact and shear, not compression alone: the teeth literally tear the particles apart.
  3. Hence suited to weak, ductile or soft materials such as coal, which smooth rolls would only squeeze.
  4. More versatile: one toothed roll can work against a stationary curved breaker plate.

Limitation: they cannot handle very hard solids; smooth rolls give few fines and virtually no oversize.
pts: Smooth rolls act by compression only and are limited by nip (\cos\alpha = (R + d/2)/(R + r), angle of nip about 32°), so the feed is only a few times the gap (about 4 for 1 m rolls set 12.5 mm apart)
Toothed rolls are not limited by nip and can reduce much larger particles (feed up to about 500 mm)
Toothed rolls break by compression, impact and shear; the teeth tear the particles apart
Suited to weak, ductile or soft materials such as coal
More versatile (single roll against a breaker plate), with the limitation that very hard solids cannot be handled
6c.src: Size reduction, slides 19-22; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 8-9; Standard textbook treatment
6c.watch:
• The question asks for advantages; a sentence on the limitation (no very hard solids) shows judgement but should stay short.
  • The example numbers (1 m rolls, 12.5 mm gap, 2\alpha = 32^\circ) are illustrative; the nip condition \tan\alpha \le \mu needs \mu of about 0.29.

6d.fix: • Slide 5 gives cone crushers as the typical equipment of the grinding stage. A cone crusher is a secondary crusher, as slide 18 itself says; grinding below about 6 mm is done in tumbling mills (rod and ball mills).
6d.html:
Size reduction is done in stages, each with its own machines:

  1. Primary (coarse) crushers: jaw crushers (Blake, Dodge) and gyratory crushers; run-of-mine boulders down to about 0.5 to 6 in.
  2. Secondary crushers: cone crushers, roll crushers (smooth and toothed) and stamp mills; down to about 6 mm.
  3. Grinding (tumbling or revolving) mills: rod mills, ball mills and autogenous mills; below 6 mm down to micrometres.

In the general chemical-engineering grouping the principal types are crushers, grinders, ultrafine grinders (fluid-energy and agitated mills) and cutting machines (knife cutters).
pts: Primary crushers: jaw (Blake, Dodge) and gyratory crushers
Secondary crushers: cone crushers, smooth and toothed roll crushers (stamp mills also credited)
Grinding (tumbling) mills: rod, ball and autogenous mills
Gives the product size range of each stage, or names ultrafine grinders and cutting machines

7a.fix:
• The paper prints the head weight as 200 g; the data match only a 2000 g head (the assays imply 1925 g), as in the course example on slide 16.
  • Slide 17 writes the recovery denominator as 0.21 \times 2000; it must be 0.021 \times 2000 = 42 g of Pb for the printed 91.83%.
7a.html:
Given: head 200 g (as printed) at f = 2.1\% Pb; concentrate C = 70 g at c = 55.1\% Pb; tailing t = 0.1\% Pb.

Find: ratio of concentration, recovery and theoretical head assay.

Step 1, consistency check. Pb in the concentrate = 70 \times 0.551 = 38.57 g, but Pb in a 200 g head = 200 \times 0.021 = 4.2 g. The concentrate cannot hold nine times the lead of the feed (recovery would be 918%), so the head weight is a misprint. The assays fix it:

F = C\,\frac{c - t}{f - t} = 70 \times \frac{0.550}{0.020} = 1925\ \mathrm{g} \approx 2000\ \mathrm{g}

This is the course test with a 2000 g head, used below.

Step 2, ratio of concentration:

K = \frac{F}{C} = \frac{2000}{70} = 28.6

Step 3, recovery:

R = \frac{Cc}{Ff}\times 100 = \frac{38.57}{2000 \times 0.021}\times 100 = \frac{38.57}{42.0}\times 100 = 91.8\%

Step 4, theoretical head assay. Tailing by difference T = 2000 - 70 = 1930 g:

\text{head assay} = \frac{Cc + Tt}{F}\times 100 = \frac{38.57 + 1930 \times 0.001}{2000}\times 100 = \frac{40.50}{2000}\times 100 = 2.025\%\ \mathrm{Pb}

Answer: ratio of concentration 28.6 to 1, recovery 91.8%, theoretical head assay 2.03% Pb (against 2.1% measured). From the assays alone, which do not depend on the misprinted weight: 27.5 to 1 and 95.4%. Taken as printed (200 g), the same steps give 2.86 to 1, 918% and 19.35% Pb.
pts: Notes that the printed 200 g head is inconsistent (38.57 g Pb in the concentrate against 4.2 g in the head; recovery over 100% is impossible), then uses 2000 g or the assay-only formulas

K = 2000/70 = 28.6 to 1 (or (c - t)/(f - t) = 27.5 to 1; 2.86 with the printed 200 g)
Pb in concentrate 38.57 g and in head 42.0 g (4.2 g with the printed 200 g)
Recovery = 91.8\% (or 95.4% from the two-product formula; 918% with the printed 200 g)
Tailing weight by difference, 1930 g, and Pb in tailing 1.93 g (130 g and 0.13 g with the printed 200 g)
Theoretical head assay as (metal in concentrate + metal in tailing) / weight of ore

  • The theoretical (calculated) head differs from the assayed 2.1% because of sampling, weighing and assay errors; this is why the assay-based recovery (95.4%) differs from the weight-based one.

7b.html:
Screening sizes particles with a physical barrier: undersize falls through the apertures, oversize moves across the surface.

Purposes.

  1. Size control in comminution circuits: for minus ½ inch ball-mill feed, the roll product is screened at ½ inch; undersize goes to the mill, oversize returns to the rolls. This prevents oversize passing on and avoids overgrinding.
  2. Scalping: bar screens ahead of coarse crushers remove material that is already fine enough, raising crusher capacity.
  3. Preparing sized feed for concentration (jigs, tables) and sizing final products to specification.

Factors affecting performance.

  1. Feed rate: a low feed rate and long screening time give almost complete separation, but high rates make a thick bed the fines must cross; capacity and efficiency oppose each other.
  2. Probability of hitting the screen matrix: only the open area passes particles, P = [(D_A - d)/(D_A + D_W)]^2 per presentation, so particles need many presentations; more open area raises it.
  3. Blinding: particles just larger than the aperture block it; screen motion (vertical and horizontal) frees them.
  4. Angle of approach and shape: perpendicular approach passes best; plate-like mica rides over the apertures.
  5. Nature of the feed: much near-mesh material lowers efficiency, as in closed circuit with crushers.
  6. Moisture: damp feed agglomerates and blinds; screen perfectly dry or wet, never damp. Wet screening is most efficient but needs dewatering.
pts: Purpose: size control in crushing and grinding circuits, for example the ½ inch roll product with oversize returned (closed circuit)
A further purpose: scalping before crushers, or sized feed for concentration, or product sizing
Feed rate: capacity and efficiency are opposing; high rates give a thick bed and lower efficiency
Probability of hitting the screen matrix and open area; particles need many presentations
Blinding by near-mesh particles, relieved by screen motion
Angle of approach and particle shape or orientation (mica rides over)
Nature of the feed: near-mesh material lowers efficiency
Moisture: damp feeds agglomerate and blind; screen dry or wet, never damp; wet screening most efficient but costly to dewater

  • Screen efficiency is judged from the mass balance: recovery of oversize to the overflow times recovery of undersize to the underflow.

7c.html:
Classification is a method of separating mineral particles of various sizes, shapes and specific gravities into two or more products on the basis of the velocity with which they fall through a fluid (usually water: wet classifying). Coarse, heavier and rounder grains settle faster than finer, lighter and more angular ones. It is used for particles too fine to be screened efficiently.

Principle.

  1. Terminal velocity. Gravity (less buoyancy) accelerates a particle, while the fluid resistance rises with velocity. When they balance, the particle reaches its terminal velocity and falls uniformly.
  2. Resistance. At low velocity it is viscous (shear); at high velocity turbulent (fluid displacement). In the viscous range Stokes' law applies:
v_t = \frac{d^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)\,g}{18\,\mu}

For equal density the larger particle falls faster; for equal size the denser one does.

  1. Sorting column. Fluid rises at a uniform velocity V: particles with v_t > V sink to the spigot, those with v_t < V go to the overflow.
  2. Size and density together. In water at 20 degrees C (\mu = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}), 50 μm quartz (2.7) settles at 2.3 mm/s and 50 μm galena (7.5) at 8.9 mm/s, so galena of 50 μm reports with quartz of about 98 μm.
  3. Free and hindered settling. Below about 15% solids, particles settle freely and size dominates (horizontal-current, sedimentation classifiers). In denser pulps crowding makes the pulp act as a heavy liquid; this hindered settling raises the effect of density (vertical-current classifiers).
pts: Defines classification: separation into two or more products by settling velocity in a fluid, which depends on size, specific gravity and shape
Coarse, heavy, round grains settle faster; used for particles too fine to screen
Gravity against resistance rising with velocity; at balance, terminal velocity and uniform fall
Viscous and turbulent resistance; Stokes' law or the rule that larger or denser particles settle faster
Sorting column (described or sketched): fluid rising at V; v_t > V to the spigot, v_t < V to the overflow
Example showing size and density act together (equal-settling 50 μm galena and about 98 μm quartz)
Free settling (below about 15% solids, size dominant) and hindered settling (density effect increased) and the classifier types that use them

• Column with fluid rising at V; overflow (v_t < V, fine, light) at the top, spigot product (v_t > V, coarse, dense) at the bottom.
  • Particle with weight down and buoyancy and drag up.

7c.watch:
• The question has two parts: a one-sentence definition, then the mechanism. The terminal velocity and the sorting column carry most of the "principle" marks.
  • Stokes' law holds only for fine particles (small Reynolds number, below roughly 50 to 100 μm in water); coarser particles pass through an intermediate range into the turbulent (Newton) regime, reached at a few millimetres.

8a.html:
Why drying is expensive

Thickening is the cheapest dewatering method (40-50 % water left), filtration is dearer (about 10 %), drying is the dearest (zero).

  1. Thickening and filtration remove water as a liquid, mechanically: gravity settling (slow rakes, almost no power or attendance, so the cost is mainly capital) and a pressure difference across a filter cloth. No phase change.
  2. Drying must convert the water to vapour: heat raises the water to its boiling point and supplies the large latent heat of evaporation (2257 kJ/kg at 100 C), about 2.57 MJ per kg of water from 25 C, all from fuel.
  3. Heat is also lost to the solids and the hot exit gas, and the gas raises dust.

Per tonne of dry solids, a 10 % filter cake holds 111 kg of water (about 0.29 GJ to evaporate); a 45 % thickener underflow holds 818 kg (about 2.1 GJ). So the cheap methods remove most water, and drying only the last part that smelting and shipping require.

Drying in a rotary cylindrical dryer

  1. Shell: sheet-steel cylinder, 5-30 m long, 0.9-3.0 m in diameter, sloping 3-5 degrees, on rollers, turned at 1.5-2 rpm by a drive gear.
  2. Wet material is fed continuously at the raised end.
  3. Lifting flights (shelves) turn the material over and over through the gas and stop it sticking; with the slope it moves toward the discharge end.
  4. Hot gases (750-1000 C) from burning fuel enter at the discharge end and flow counter-current, leaving cool and moist at the feed end.
  5. The hottest, driest gas meets the nearly dry solids, so the last traces of moisture are removed efficiently, and heat use is good.
  6. Dry solids leave continuously at the lower end.
pts: Gives the comparison: thickening cheapest (40-50 % water), filtration more expensive (about 10 %), drying most expensive (zero water)
Thickening and filtration remove liquid water mechanically (gravity, pressure difference) with little energy; thickening cost is mainly capital
Drying must evaporate the water: sensible heat plus the large latent heat of evaporation (about 2260 kJ/kg), supplied by fuel
Extra heat losses (hot exit gas, heating the solids) or dust formation
Concludes that cheap mechanical dewatering is done first and drying removes only the last water, which later steps require (or a worked energy figure)
Construction: steel cylinder 5-30 m long, 0.9-3.0 m diameter, slope 3-5 degrees, on rollers, 1.5-2 rpm
Lifting flights or shelves turn the material over through the gas and stop it sticking; it moves toward the discharge end
Wet feed charged continuously at the raised end; dry product leaves at the lower end
Hot gases (750-1000 C) flow counter-current, so the hottest, driest gas removes the last traces of moisture efficiently
Moist, cooled gas leaves at the feed end

8b.html:
In froth flotation, hydrophobic particles attach to rising air bubbles and are skimmed off in the froth; hydrophilic particles stay in the pulp. Most minerals are ionically or covalently bonded and hydrophilic, so reagents are used.

Collectors. Heteropolar organic compounds: the polar group adsorbs on the selected mineral and the non-polar hydrocarbon chain points into the water. The surface the water sees is hydrocarbon, so the mineral becomes water-repellent and attaches to bubbles. Example: sodium ethyl xanthate, \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2Na} (100-750 g/t), dissociates, and the -\mathrm{S^-} of \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2^-} bonds to the cations of a sulphide surface (galena). Role: they create the selective hydrophobicity.

Frothers. Surface-active heteropolar reagents (pine oil, cresylic acid; 50-300 g/t) that adsorb at the air-water interface, polar group in the water, and lower the surface tension. Role: stable bubbles and a froth that carries the mineral to the surface without bursting; too stable a froth is hard to handle. They have practically no effect on floatability.

Activators. Modifiers that make a mineral surface more amenable to the collector. Sphalerite responds weakly to xanthate because zinc xanthate is fairly soluble; \mathrm{CuSO_4} replaces surface \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} by \mathrm{Cu^{2+}},

\mathrm{ZnS(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow CuS(s) + Zn^{2+}(aq)}

and xanthate then adsorbs strongly, so sphalerite floats.

Depressors (depressants). Modifiers with the opposite role: they make a surface inactive to the collector. In a galena-chalcocite (\mathrm{Cu_2S}) pulp, NaCN forms a stable copper cyanide complex at the copper-mineral surface, while lead cyanide is unstable; xanthate adsorbs only on galena, which floats while the copper mineral stays in the pulp. Lime at high pH similarly depresses pyrite.

Activators and depressors together make the collector selective, so complex ores are floated one mineral at a time.
pts: States the principle: hydrophobic particles attach to bubbles and float; most minerals are hydrophilic, so reagents are needed
Collector: heteropolar, polar group adsorbs on the mineral, non-polar chain faces the water, making the mineral hydrophobic
Collector example: xanthate, whose -\mathrm{S^-} bonds to sulphide surface cations
Frother: adsorbs at the air-water interface and lowers the surface tension, with an example (pine oil, cresylic acid)
Frother role: stable bubbles and froth carry the mineral up; not too stable; little effect on the mineral
Activator: makes the surface amenable to the collector, with \mathrm{CuSO_4} on sphalerite (\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} replaces \mathrm{Zn^{2+}})
Depressor: makes the surface inactive to the collector, with NaCN on the copper sulphide so galena floats (or lime on pyrite)
